reels.title: The night Ussher said the world began

prediction.prompt: By Ussher's date the world would be about 6,000 years old. How old does radiometric dating make Earth?

frames.text: James Ussher, Archbishop of Armagh, calculated that the world began at nightfall before 23 October, 4004 BC.
frames.say: James Usher, Archbishop of Armah, calculated that the world began at nightfall before the twenty-third of October, four thousand and four B C.

frames.text: He published the date in 1650, in his Annals of the Old Testament.
It took real learning: ancient history, astronomy, old calendars and the languages of the Bible.
Where he had several sources beyond the Bible, his dates usually hold up. He put the death of Julius Caesar in 44 BC.
frames.say: Where he had several sources beyond the Bible, his dates usually hold up. He put the death of Julius Caesar in forty-four B C.

frames.text: Radiometric dating puts Earth's age at about 4.54 billion years.
frames.say: Radiometric dating puts Earth's age at about four point five four billion years.

reels.takeaway: Ussher counted back through written records to 4004 BC. Radiometric dating puts Earth's age at about 4.54 billion years.

claims.claim: Ussher dated the Creation to the start of the night before 23 October 4004 BC
claims.quote: the entrance of the night preceding the 23rd day of October ... the year before Christ 4004

claims.claim: His Annals of the Old Testament appeared in 1650
claims.quote: the Annales veteris testamenti, a prima mundi origine deducti ("Annals of the Old Testament, deduced from the first origins of the world"), which appeared in 1650

claims.claim: The chronology needed ancient history, the Bible and its languages, astronomy and ancient calendars
claims.quote: it demanded great depth of learning in what was then known of ancient history, including the rise of the Persians, Greeks and Romans, as well as expertise in the Bible, biblical languages, astronomy, ancient calendars and chronology

claims.claim: Where he had several sources besides the Bible, his dates usually agree with modern ones, such as Caesar's death in 44 BC
claims.quote: Ussher's account of historical events for which he had multiple sources other than the Bible is usually in close agreement with modern accounts – for example, he placed the death of Alexander in 323 BC and that of Julius Caesar in 44 BC.

claims.claim: Earth is estimated to be about 4.54 billion years old
claims.quote: The age of Earth is estimated to be 4.54 ± 0.05 billion years.

claims.claim: The estimate rests on radiometric dating of meteorites
claims.quote: Estimates are based on radiometric dating of meteoritic material

reels.title: A storm that grew in a day

prediction.prompt: This storm, seen from space on 23 October 2015, set a world record that day. Which one?

choices.label: Strongest sustained winds of any tropical cyclone
Most rain in a single day

frames.text: A storm closes on the Pacific coast of Mexico, photographed by a satellite on 23 October 2015.
This is Hurricane Patricia. In a single day it strengthened from tropical storm to Category 5.
Its sustained winds reached about 345 kilometres an hour, the highest ever reliably measured or estimated in a tropical cyclone.
Near its peak it turned toward land, and weakened fast. It came ashore near Cuixmala, Jalisco, with winds of about 240 kilometres an hour.
frames.say: Near its peak it turned toward land, and weakened fast. It came ashore near Kweesh-mah-la, Ha-lees-ko, with winds of about two hundred and forty kilometres an hour.

frames.text: Mexico's mountains broke it up. Within 24 hours of landfall it was a tropical depression.

reels.takeaway: In about a day and a half Patricia went from tropical storm to the strongest sustained winds reliably measured or estimated in a tropical cyclone, and it faded within a day of landfall.

claims.claim: The satellite image shows Patricia just after its peak, nearing western Mexico on 23 October 2015
claims.quote: Hurricane Patricia shortly after peak intensity and approaching Western Mexico on October 23, 2015.

claims.claim: Patricia went from tropical storm to Category 5 hurricane in 24 hours
claims.quote: Patricia grew from a tropical storm to a Category 5 hurricane in just 24 hours

claims.claim: On 23 October its maximum sustained winds peaked at 345 km/h
claims.quote: On October 23, the hurricane achieved its record peak intensity with maximum sustained winds of 215 mph (345 km/h).

claims.claim: Its one-minute sustained winds are the highest ever reliably observed or estimated in a tropical cyclone
claims.quote: Patricia's one-minute maximum sustained winds ranked as the highest ever reliably observed or estimated in a tropical cyclone

claims.claim: Near its peak it turned towards Mexico
claims.quote: As Patricia neared its peak strength, the cyclone began to turn east-northeast towards Mexico.

claims.claim: After dramatic weakening it made landfall near Cuixmala, Jalisco, with 240 km/h winds
claims.quote: Late on October 23, dramatic weakening ensued and Patricia made landfall near Cuixmala, Jalisco, with winds of 150 mph (240 km/h).

claims.claim: It weakened very fast over Mexico's mountainous terrain
claims.quote: Patricia continued to weaken extremely quickly, faster than it had intensified, as it interacted with the mountainous terrain of Mexico.

claims.claim: Within 24 hours of landfall it was a tropical depression
claims.quote: Within 24 hours of moving ashore, Patricia weakened into a tropical depression

reels.title: The first aeroplane flight an official body certified

prediction.prompt: On 23 October 1906 Alberto Santos-Dumont took off in this biplane, the 14-bis. How far did it fly?

frames.text: This is the 14-bis, a biplane Alberto Santos-Dumont designed and built.
frames.say: This is the fourteen-bees, a biplane Alberto Santos-Doomon designed and built.

frames.text: Paris, 23 October 1906: it flew about 60 metres, a few metres up, with no catapult or ramp.
frames.say: Paris, the twenty-third of October, nineteen oh-six: it flew about sixty metres, a few metres up, with no catapult or ramp.

frames.text: On 12 November a crowd watched him fly 220 metres in 21 seconds. This photo is from that day.
France's Aero-Club certified the 12 November flight, and the world body for air records recognised it as the first of its kind.
Brazil counts him a national hero, and many there hold he beat the Wright brothers to showing a practical aeroplane.
The first powered, controlled aeroplane to fly was the Wright brothers' Flyer. Santos-Dumont made the first aeroplane flight that a record body certified.
frames.say: The first powered, controlled aeroplane to fly was the Wright brothers' Flyer. Santos-Doomon made the first aeroplane flight that a record body certified.

reels.takeaway: The Wright Flyer flew first. Santos-Dumont's 14-bis made the first aeroplane flight that an official body certified.

claims.claim: On 23 October 1906, at the Bagatelle Gamefield in Paris, the 14-bis flew about 60 metres a few metres up, taking off without a launch system
claims.quote: on 23 October 1906 flew about 60 metres at a height of two to three metres with the fixed-wing 14-bis (also dubbed the Oiseau de proie—"bird of prey") at the Bagatelle Gamefield in Paris, taking off unassisted by an external launch system.

claims.claim: The 14-bis was a canard biplane Santos-Dumont designed and built
claims.quote: was a pioneer era, canard-style biplane designed and built by Brazilian aviation pioneer Alberto Santos-Dumont

claims.claim: It took off without ramps, catapults or other devices
claims.quote: The plane lifted off and flew for 60 metres, without taking advantage of headwinds, ramps, catapults, slopes, or other devices.

claims.claim: On 12 November, before a crowd, he flew 220 metres
claims.quote: On 12 November in front of a crowd, he flew 220 metres at a height of six metres.

claims.claim: The 220-metre flight lasted 21 seconds
claims.quote: he took off against the wind and flew 220 metres, for 21 seconds at an average speed of 37.4 km/h

claims.claim: They were the first heavier-than-air flights certified by the Aeroclub of France, and the first of their kind recognised by the FAI
claims.quote: These were the first heavier-than-air flights certified by the Aeroclub of France, the first such flights officially witnessed by an aeronautics recordkeeping body, and the first of their kind recognised by the Fédération Aéronautique Internationale.

claims.claim: He is a national hero in Brazil, where many hold he preceded the Wright brothers
claims.quote: Santos-Dumont is a national hero in Brazil, where it is popularly held that he preceded the Wright brothers in demonstrating a practical aeroplane.

claims.claim: The Wright Flyer was the first powered, controlled aeroplane to fly
claims.quote: The first powered, controlled aeroplane to fly, the Wright Flyer, used a biplane wing arrangement

reels.title: Only a theory

prediction.prompt: When scientists call evolution a theory, what do they mean?

choices.label: A tested explanation of the facts
A fact proved beyond any doubt

frames.text: Evolution is often waved away as only a theory, as if a theory were an opinion or a hunch.
In science the word means something much stronger: a well-supported explanation of the facts.
Before it counts, it must survive repeated tests that try to prove it wrong.
The facts come from fossils that record transitions, from traces of shared ancestry in living things, and from change seen happening now.
That is why many scientists call evolution both a fact and a theory. The evidence for it keeps being tested.

reels.takeaway: In science a theory is not a guess. It is the tested explanation that ties the facts together.

claims.claim: To the public 'theory' can mean an opinion; to scientists it means a well-substantiated explanation
claims.quote: To the public, theory can mean an opinion or conjecture (e.g., "it's only a theory"), but among scientists it has a much stronger connotation of "well-substantiated explanation".

claims.claim: A scientific theory is a well-substantiated explanation of some aspect of the natural world
claims.quote: A scientific theory is "a well-substantiated explanation of some aspect of the natural world that can incorporate facts, laws, inferences, and tested hypotheses."

claims.claim: Theories come from hypotheses tested repeatedly by attempts to disprove them
claims.quote: Theories are formed from hypotheses that have been subjected repeatedly to tests of evidence which attempt to disprove or falsify them.

claims.claim: The facts of evolution come from current processes, traces of common descent and fossil transitions
claims.quote: The facts of evolution come from observational evidence of current processes, from imperfections in organisms recording historical common descent, and from transitions in the fossil record.

claims.claim: Many scientists and philosophers of science describe evolution as fact and theory
claims.quote: Many scientists and philosophers of science have described evolution as fact and theory

claims.claim: Evidence for evolution continues to be gathered and tested
claims.quote: Evidence for evolution continues to be accumulated and tested.

reels.title: Naming the Great Pestilence

prediction.prompt: Medieval England called it the Great Pestilence. How do we know which disease it really was?

choices.label: Doctors at the time named it
DNA from skeletons in a plague cemetery
Rat bones found in old cellars

frames.text: England, 1348. A plague arrives that halts the campaigns of the Hundred Years' War and kills an estimated 40 to 60 percent of the people.
frames.say: England, thirteen forty-eight. A plague arrives that halts the campaigns of the Hundred Years' War and kills an estimated forty to sixty percent of the people.

frames.text: People at the time called it the Great Pestilence or the Great Mortality. The name Black Death came centuries later.
Key proof of what it was came from London, from a cemetery at East Smithfield dug for the Black Death's dead.
In 2011, scientists reported DNA of Yersinia pestis, the plague bacterium, in skeletons from that cemetery.
frames.say: In twenty eleven, scientists reported DNA of Yersinia pestis, the plague bacterium, in skeletons from that cemetery.

frames.text: Its genes showed a strain that was new at the time. Many modern plague strains descend from it.
A new strain probably met bodies with little or no defence against it. That may help explain why so many died.

reels.takeaway: The dead themselves named the killer: DNA from their skeletons showed Yersinia pestis, in a strain new at the time.

claims.claim: Its most immediate consequence was a halt to the Hundred Years' War campaigns
claims.quote: The most immediate consequence was a halt to the campaigns of the Hundred Years' War.

claims.claim: An estimated 40–60% of England's population died
claims.quote: a figure of 40–60% of the population is widely accepted

claims.claim: Contemporaries called it the Great Pestilence or the Great Mortality, not the Black Death
claims.quote: was not used by contemporaries, who preferred such names as the "Great Pestilence" or the "Great Mortality"

claims.claim: The name Black Death became common only centuries later
claims.quote: It was not until the 17th century that the term under which we know the outbreak today became common

claims.claim: A 2011 study found Yersinia pestis DNA in skeletons from the Black Death cemetery in East Smithfield, London
claims.quote: A study reported in 2011 of skeletons exhumed from the Black Death cemetery in East Smithfield, London, found Yersinia pestis DNA.

claims.claim: Plague is caused by Yersinia pestis bacteria
claims.quote: It is generally agreed today that the disease in question was plague, caused by Yersinia pestis bacteria.

claims.claim: Genotyping showed a then newly evolved strain, ancestral to modern strains
claims.quote: Genotyping showed that it was [at that time] a newly evolved strain, ancestor of all modern strains

claims.claim: Modern medicine suggests a new strain met immune systems with little or no defence, which may help explain the high death rates
claims.quote: because it was a new strain, the human immune system would have had little or no defence against it, helping to explain the plague's virulence and high death rates

prediction.prompt: On 23 October 1295 Scotland and France signed an alliance against England. Which side did it favour?

choices.label: Neither: it was an equal deal

frames.text: Paris, 23 October 1295. Scottish envoys sign a treaty with France against England.
frames.say: Paris, the twenty-third of October, twelve ninety-five. Scottish envoys sign a treaty with France against England.

frames.text: If England attacked either country, the other would invade English territory.
It favoured France. The French had only to keep fighting the English in Gascony.
It did not protect Scotland. In 1296 Edward I invaded, and Scottish independence nearly ended.
frames.say: It did not protect Scotland. In twelve ninety-six Edward the First invaded, and Scottish independence nearly ended.

frames.text: The bond was renewed for centuries. In 1558 Mary, Queen of Scots, married the future Francis II of France.

frames.text: The alliance was never formally revoked. Scotland and France still play rugby for an Auld Alliance Trophy.

reels.takeaway: Scotland and France allied against England in 1295, and the Auld Alliance was never formally revoked.

reels.title: Whose words were they

prediction.prompt: Who first wrote the phrase "survival of the fittest"?

frames.text: "Survival of the fittest" sounds like Darwin. The words are Herbert Spencer's, from 1864.
frames.say: Survival of the fittest sounds like Darwin. The words are Herbert Spencer's, from eighteen sixty-four.

frames.text: Spencer said his phrase meant what Darwin had called natural selection.
How do we know Darwin borrowed it? His letters. In July 1866 Wallace wrote to him with a worry.
frames.say: How do we know Darwin borrowed it? His letters. In July eighteen sixty-six Wallace wrote to him with a worry.

frames.text: Readers took "natural selection" to mean that nature chooses. Spencer's words, Wallace said, avoided that.
Darwin replied that the phrase's advantages had not occurred to him until that letter. He added it to the fifth edition of On the Origin of Species, in 1869.
frames.say: Darwin replied that the phrase's advantages had not occurred to him until that letter. He added it to the fifth edition of On the Origin of Species, in eighteen sixty-nine.

frames.text: In biology, fittest does not mean strongest. It is best understood as the form that leaves the most copies of itself.

reels.takeaway: Survival of the fittest was Spencer's phrase. Darwin's letters show when and why he borrowed it.

claims.claim: Herbert Spencer first used the phrase, in Principles of Biology (1864)
claims.quote: Herbert Spencer first used the phrase, after reading Charles Darwin's On the Origin of Species, in his Principles of Biology (1864)

claims.claim: Spencer equated his phrase with Darwin's natural selection
claims.quote: This survival of the fittest, which I have here sought to express in mechanical terms, is that which Mr. Darwin has called 'natural selection'

claims.claim: In July 1866 Wallace wrote that readers took 'natural selection' to personify nature, and suggested Spencer's term
claims.quote: In July 1866, Alfred Russel Wallace wrote to Darwin about readers thinking that the phrase "natural selection" personified nature as "selecting" and said this misconception could be avoided "by adopting Spencer's term"

claims.claim: Darwin replied that the advantages of Spencer's phrase had not occurred to him till he read Wallace's letter
claims.quote: I fully agree with all that you say on the advantages of H. Spencer's excellent expression of 'the survival of the fittest'. This however had not occurred to me till reading your letter.

claims.claim: Darwin introduced the phrase in the fifth edition of the Origin, 1869
claims.quote: In On the Origin of Species, he introduced the phrase in the fifth edition published in 1869

claims.claim: In Darwinian terms it means survival of the form that leaves most copies of itself
claims.quote: In Darwinian terms, the phrase is best understood as "survival of the form that in successive generations will leave most copies of itself."
